articles.title: In 2023, an Ontario court banned backyard burning after neighbours complained of smoke; three years later, repeated incidents ended with a ban on barbecues and any fire-producing device
articles.summary: An Ontario court has banned a man from using a barbecue and any fire-producing devices on his property following persistent complaints from neighbors about smoke. The ruling comes after a three-year dispute involving multiple instances of smoke emissions affecting the neighbors' enjoyment of their homes.
articles.body: An Ontario man at the centre of a three-year dispute with his neighbours has been barred from using a barbecue or any other fire-producing device on his property after repeated complaints about smoke.A Superior Court of Justice judge in Sault Ste. Marie issued an injunction in May 2023 prohibiting the man from burning firewood or “any other substances or materials” on or around his property. The order was made “absolute and without exception” after concerns that the defendant might circumvent its restrictions.Court issues strict backyard fire banThe case initially focused on smoke from the man's backyard. In June 2023, his lawyer asked whether the injunction could be changed to allow him to use his barbecue.The plaintiffs opposed the request but told the court that the order was not intended to prevent normal use of a natural gas barbecue.The court later found that the man used the barbecue in ways that went beyond cooking.On two occasions in July 2023, he cooked dinner and then left the barbecue burning and producing smoke for about 90 minutes without attending to it or preparing any food, according to the judgment, as cited by CTV News.The smoke affected the neighbours' ability to enjoy their property without exposure to smoke, the judge said.In September that year, the man also lit a propane-fuelled fire in his backyard without an apparent cooking purpose.Barbecue use leads to further complaintsThe neighbours later opposed another request to allow barbecue use, saying they had “no confidence your client will not use his barbecue to create a nuisance.”In November, the man's lawyer asked the court to permit barbecue use solely for cooking and eating. The request was not approved.The dispute over the wording of the injunction continued. In February 2024, the man wrote to the plaintiffs' lawyer saying he intended to use his barbecue and other appliances powered by liquid petroleum gas.He argued that the injunction did not cover liquid petroleum gas because he considered it a mixture rather than a “substance”.The man began representing himself later that month.Smoke-producing machineryThe complaints later extended beyond the barbecue.In April 2024, the man started a piece of machinery on his patio six times during one day. The equipment released a large amount of smoke, according to the court decision.The activity was frequent enough that another neighbour submitted an affidavit raising concerns about the smoke.In May 2024, the man was accused of revving a vehicle engine for about two hours while releasing a large amount of smoke.The plaintiffs' lawyer then asked the court to find the man in contempt.The judge concluded that the man understood the injunction, even though he disagreed with it.The court considered the prolonged barbecue use, propane fire, smoke-producing machinery and vehicle engine to be conduct that violated the purpose of the order.“I can think of no reason the defendant did this except to intentionally disrupt the enjoyment of the plaintiffs,” the judge wrote. “The defendant used his barbecue as a weapon of nuisance, in direct violation of the injunctive order.”Judge declines contempt findingThe judge found there were grounds for contempt but decided not to make a contempt finding.The decision noted that the man had complied with the injunction for more than two years after learning that he could face contempt proceedings for violating it.The judge said that continued compliance was expected and warned the man against trying to interpret the order in a way that would undermine its purpose.“It is the expectation of this court that the defendant will continue to comply with the injunction order and not resort back to playing games and interpreting the injunction order in ways that suit his intention to disrupt the enjoyment of the plaintiffs,” the judge said.The injunction remains in force, leaving the man prohibited from burning materials or using fire-producing devices in the manner covered by the order.You use AI every day. articles.title: MEA condemns attacks on seafarers in Black Sea, says targeting of shipping must end
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The Ministry of External Affairs (Mea) on Wednesday condemned a string of attacks on commercial vessels in the Black Sea region, including
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Ministry of External Affairs (Mea) on Wednesday condemned a string of attacks on commercial vessels in the Black Sea region, including ships carrying Indian seafarers. India called for an immediate end to attacks that threaten commercial shipping and endanger the lives of seafarers.Mea spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said India was monitoring the situation and assisting Indian nationals affected by the attacks.“We have seen a string of attacks in the Black Sea region in the last one or two days. We condemn such attacks that threaten commercial shipping and endanger the lives of our seafaring community,” Jaiswal said at a bi-weekly media briefing.Jaiswal said the commercial vessel MV Royad Mammadov came under attack while sailing in the Black Sea. Three Indian nationals were on board, all of whom were safe, though one was injured and receiving medical treatment.“We condemn such attacks that threaten commercial shipping and endanger, first, the commercial vessel MV Royad Mammadov came under attack while it was sailing in the Black Sea. There were three Indian nationals on board. All of them are safe, but one of them got injured and is receiving medical treatment. We thank Romanian authorities for lending a helping hand in this particular incident,” Jaiswal said.“The second ship that came under attack was Alfa Watan. This is a Togo-flagged ship. It came under attack yesterday and the fate of its crew is unknown at this point.”He further mentioned that another vessel, the Palau-flagged MV Able, came under a drone attack, but all 18 crew members, including seven Indian nationals, were rescued. “One Indian national has been injured and is receiving medical assistance and supervision,” he said, thanking Bulgarian authorities for their timely help. Jaiswal added that the Indian mission in Sofia was offering “all possible assistance” to the country’s seafarers.“The fourth ship, as I earlier said, that came under attack. This is a Liberian-flagged oil tanker Aframax Rio. All the crew members are Indian nationals. All 23 crew members on board this particular ship are Indian nationals and all of them have been rescued", Jaiswal said.Meanwhile, the Indian Embassy in Romania said that a representative of the Embassy met three Indian nationals rescued from the commercial vessel M V Royad Mammadov on Tuesday. Bulgaria’s prime minister had said on Tuesday two commercial vessels were struck by drones on Tuesday in the first such attack on shipping in the Nato member’s exclusive economic zone in the Black Sea.“This is an unacceptable attack in Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone. It is a blatant violation of international law and maritime law,” he said. Jaiswal also said India would continue to assist affected seafarers and reiterated New Delhi’s call for an immediate de-escalation of tensions.“We once again reiterate our calls for dialogue and diplomacy to de-escalate tensions. The targeting of shipping seafarers in the region must end and free and unimpeded navigation through international waterways must be restored at the earliest,” the spokesperson said.On Tuesday, the ministry had expressed grave concern over continuing threats to merchant vessels and seafarers in the region, warning that such attacks could have wider consequences for global commerce and the welfare of people worldwide.The Mea also highlighted India’s role in co-launching the “Group of Friends on Safety and Security of Shipping and Seafarers” at the United Nations, highlighting New Delhi’s focus on the protection of maritime trade and those working aboard commercial vessels. External affairs minister S Jaishankar had separately flagged the issue during his address to the United Nations General Assembly the previous week, where he raised concerns over attacks targeting commercial shipping and stressed the need to safeguard freedom of navigation.The repeated warnings come as concerns over maritime security continue to grow.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Eleven arrested at pro-Palestinian marches in London on 7 October
articles.summary: Five people were arrested for inciting racial hatred at a protest outside the office of the Board of Deputies of British Jews, the Met says.
articles.body:
Eleven people were arrested at several pro-Palestinian demonstrations held in London on Wednesday.

Among them were five people arrested on suspicion of inciting racial hatred at a protest outside the office of the Board of Deputies of British Jews in north London, the Metropolitan Police said.

The force said the other arrests were made at student pro-Palestinian protests elsewhere in the capital, which were held despite calls for them to be postponed.

Wednesday marked three years since the 7 October attack on Israel by Hamas, in which around 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken as hostages by the militant group.

Israel responded to the attack by launching a military offensive in Gaza that has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians, according to the Hamas-run health ministry.

Footage from the demonstration outside the Board of Deputies' Camden office showed a few dozen protesters, several of whom were wearing face coverings.

In a statement following the arrests, the Board of Deputies, the UK's largest Jewish community group, said it "would not be threatened or intimidated" and thanked police for their "swift" response.

Slogans "calling for intifada" were chanted during the protest, according to the Met. The five arrested remain in custody.

The term intifada came into popular use during the Palestinian uprising against Israeli occupation of the West Bank and Gaza Strip in 1987.

Jewish groups have described the term as a call for violence against Jewish people. Pro-Palestinian groups have said it is a call for peaceful resistance to Israel's occupation.

The Board of Deputies held a vigil in Whitehall, central London, later on Wednesday to remember the victims of the 7 October attack.

In a later statement, the Met said officers would remain on the ground in central London for the remainder of the afternoon.

A pro-Palestinian march attended by around 100 people took place between Lincoln's Inn Fields to Russell Square.

The Met had previously called for the student protest to take place on a different day, saying demonstrations on 7 October would cause distress on a day of mourning for Jewish students and staff.

Five were arrested for breaching conditions imposed on the march, including not to wear face coverings, the Met said.

One person was arrested on suspicion of common assault.

The Met said it ended ahead of a police-enforced dispersal time, which was imposed when organisers rejected calls to move it from 7 October.

Counter-demonstrators carrying Israeli flags also gathered in Russell Square. There were some minor scuffles between the two groups.

Pro-Palestinian protesters were heard chanting "Zionists not welcome here" and "free Palestine from the river to the sea".

Some use the chant as a call for Palestinian control of all land between the Jordan River and the Mediterranean Sea, including Israel.

Critics say the slogan is a call for the destruction of the state of Israel.

That interpretation is disputed by pro-Palestinian activists, who say that most people chanting it are calling for an end to Israel's occupation of the West Bank and blockade of Gaza, not the destruction of Israel itself.

articles.title: New OPT fee proposed: Colleges to pay $70,000 for first-time F-1 students, $30,000 for extensions; DHS says this was never meant to be a backdoor
articles.summary: The Department of Homeland Security announced a proposed rule that would impose a $70,000 fee for F-1 students seeking to participate in the OPT program
articles.body: The Department of Homeland Security announced a proposed rule that would impose a $70,000 fee for F-1 students seeking to participate in the OPT program and $30,000 for each subsequent OPT authorization including STEM OPT extensions. Schools will have to pay this fee, not the international students. The proposed rule is scheduled for publication in the Federal Register on October 8, 2026, and DHS will accept public comments for 30 days.“Optional Practical Training was never meant to be a back door into the American workforce, a subsidy for cheap labor, or a prize for those who game the system,” said a DHS Spokesperson. “DHS is upskilling OPT to require foreign students to justify their worth to employers. American workers should not have to compete against a program that has been turned into a pipeline for cheap foreign labor.”What does new DHS proposal say?Existing federal regulations allow eligible F-1 nonimmigrant students to engage in OPT if the OPT is directly related to the student’s major area of study. To participate, F-1 nonimmigrant students must receive a recommendation from their designated school official (DSO) and apply for employment authorization with U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS), the proposal said.F-1 students may apply for OPT during their academic program (pre-completion OPT) or after completing their program (post-completion OPT). Eligible F-1 nonimmigrant students may receive up to 12 months of OPT at each education level. Those who earn degrees in science, technology, engineering, or mathematics fields may be eligible for an additional 24-month extension.DHS said the proposed rule is in response to fraud and abuse identified by the Student and Exchange Visitor Program (SEVP). As more F-1 nonimmigrant students have participated in OPT, SEVP has encountered schools, designated school officials, employers, and F-1 nonimmigrant students engaged in schemes to exploit current regulations, including problematic worksites and “pay-to-stay” visa schemes.DHS believes the proposed fees would encourage schools to exercise greater oversight and selectivity when recommending F-1 nonimmigrant students for OPT, helping reduce fraud and strengthen program integrity, it said.Who will pay?DHS clarified that under the proposed rule, SEVP-certified schools must pay the fee before designated school officials recommend F-1 nonimmigrant students for OPT in the Student and Exchange Visitor Information System (SEVIS) and before F-1 nonimmigrant students apply for employment authorization with USCIS. USCIS would not grant employment authorization to F-1 nonimmigrant students if schools have not paid the required fee.The proposed fee would not be tied to a specific employer. Instead, it would apply when schools recommend an F-1 nonimmigrant student for any type of OPT. Collected fees would be deposited in the Treasury of the United States.'This will decimate our STEM talent ecosystem'Labor and mobility policy manager Sam Peak commented on the proposal saying that it will decimate America's STEM talent ecosystem. Manhattan Institute researcher Daniel Di Martino said this will be bad for innovation and will cost taxpayers.What was the earlier $100K OPT fee proposed?The $100K fee was a proposal which cleared White House review and now the DHS has published the details of it giving a clear break up of the $100K and clarifying that the schools recommending OPT for students will have to pay it.You use AI every day. articles.title: Nelson couple died in blaze after portable heater 'explosion', inquest hears
articles.summary: A fire engulfed the home after an attempt to refuel a portable heater led to a gas leak, an inquest heard.
articles.body:
An elderly couple died when a fire engulfed their home after an attempt to refuel a portable heater resulted in an "explosion".

Marlene Mumford, 84, and William Mumford, 90, died at their property at Heol Fawr, Nelson, in Caerphilly county, last December.

An inquest in Newport was told that the most likely cause of the fire was a mechanical or connection failure with the gas heater.

Assistant coroner Sarah Le Fevre said it was believed William Mumford had attempted to carry the cylinder out of the home in an effort to remove it, but that this had only caused the flames to spread.

She recorded their deaths as an accident, and the result of an "unintended act with unforeseen circumstance".

The alarm was raised by a neighbour who was in the nearby Tyler's Arms when he noticed smoke and large flames.

He and another man ran to the house where they saw a gas canister explode near the front porch with the flames rising above the height of the house.

Emergency services were initially unable to enter the property due to the extent of the damage caused by the blaze.

Firefighters reported seeing thick, black smoke "pumping out" of the property, the hearing was told.

The couple were pronounced dead at the scene.

Bridgend fire station commander Melvyn Robert Laidler said burn patterns and the location of the canister suggested William Mumford had been unable to close the cylinder and so had attempted to remove it by carrying it through the house.

A pathologist gave the cause of the couple's deaths as exposure to combustion products of fire.

"What is possible is that William realised that the fire had taken, that he realised he was unable to close the cylinder or control the fire, and therefore thought, utterly understandably, that the best course would be to try and remove the fire from the house," said the coroner.

"The fire started accidentally resulting from a mechanical or connection-related failure of a portable gas heater and gas bottle resulting in an uncontrolled gas release."

articles.title: In North Carolina, engineers built a permeable parking lot with interlocking concrete blocks; during an 88 mm storm, it produced no measured runoff
articles.summary: In a groundbreaking study, North Carolina engineers replaced traditional paving with permeable interlocking concrete blocks, achieving zero runoff during an 88mm rainstorm. Discover how this innovative approach could transform stormwater management.
articles.body: When heavy rain strikes ordinary concrete or asphalt, it typically has nowhere to go. During a major storm, water might overflow the nearby drainage system, rush across the surface, and accumulate in drains. A different strategy was explored by engineers in North Carolina, using permeable interlocking concrete pavers that let rain pass through the surface and into the stone layers beneath. During monitored rainfall events as large as 88 millimetres, the Swansboro pavement produced no measured surface runoff, according to a 2007 study in the Journal of Irrigation and Drainage Engineering.The result comes from a larger North Carolina State University study of permeable pavement across North Carolina’s Coastal Plain. The researchers weren’t just interested in whether water disappeared; they evaluated rainfall, runoff, infiltration and water quality to see where the water went. The Swansboro site was especially notable since an 88 mm rainfall storm generated no runoff from the permeable pavement.The operation of the paver systemThe Swansboro site was a 740-square-metre public overflow parking lot rather than a traffic lane. It was made of permeable interlocking concrete pavers with a thickness of 76 millimetres over stone layers, and the system was installed directly on top of sandy soil. The North Carolina State University research describes a 740-square-metre installation with 76-millimetre permeable interlocking concrete pavers over 75 millimetres of No. 72 pea gravel and 200 millimetres of No. 57 washed gravel. The washed gravel served as the stormwater storage layer, and the system was installed directly over sandy soil without a liner.The spaces between the blocks were important. Unlike the solid, sealed asphalt, the joints allowed rain to seep into the pavement rather than just sit on the surface. The coarse stone beneath the pavers then left open room for water to pool for a time before draining into the sandy soil below. Because the Swansboro system was unlined, it was meant to allow groundwater to replenish, rather than force all the stored water into a pipe.The 88-mm rain testResearchers observed the Swansboro PICP, or permeable interlocking concrete pavement, for around 10 months. The site received over 1000 mm of rainfall during this time, including five events with rainfall depths exceeding 50 mm. The biggest event was 88 millimetres of rainfall. The 2007 study in the Journal of Irrigation and Drainage Engineering found that no runoff was generated from the Swansboro location for rainfall events up to that depth.Using the SCS Curve Number method, the researchers calculated an equivalent curve number for individual rainfall events. For the site's largest monitored event, 88 mm of rain, the calculated equivalent curve number was 37. To put it plainly, the pavement was more like an extremely absorbent surface, rather than a normal paved lot, during that occurrence. The sandy soil of the site and the enormous storage layer facilitated the result. Those circumstances are important because permeable pavement relies on the underlying conditions. The speed at which stored water moved through the system depended on the soil and drainage conditions beneath the blocks.How it contrasted to typical pavementThe North Carolina investigation didn’t just look at the Swansboro pavers. Related testing monitored four permeable pavement systems, consisting of two types of permeable interlocking concrete pavement, porous concrete and concrete grid pavers, and conventional asphalt. A hydrologic study of permeable pavement and asphalt in eastern North Carolina in 2008 showed that all permeable systems considerably reduced surface runoff volumes and peak flow rates relative to asphalt.When the flow of stormwater is slowed, it lessens the abrupt pulse of water entering the downstream drainage systems. It may also provide additional chances for sediment and pollutants to filter out before water reaches groundwater or surface-water systems. The researchers also observed discrepancies among the permeable designs. The amount of water remaining in the system and the speed at which it left were affected by the open surface area, the stone beneath the pavement and the drainage arrangement.The maintenance problemPermeable pavement has an obvious weak point: the openings that let water in can also collect sediment. A 2007 field study by North Carolina researchers examined surface infiltration rates at 40 permeable pavement sites. It found that locations affected by fine sediment had much lower infiltration rates than cleaner sites. The researchers also found that simulated maintenance could substantially improve infiltration on concrete grid pavers. The result highlights an important practical point: permeable pavement is not maintenance-free simply because rain can pass through it.When soil and fine debris clog the joints or apertures, the surface can lose some of the hydraulic capacity that made it effective. So, to keep the system working properly, regular inspection and proper cleaning are part of the process.The real meaning of the 88-mm stormThe Swansboro result is impressive in that no runoff was produced from the monitored pavement. 88 mm of rain is a significant event. But the conclusion is not generalisable to all permeable pavement sites. The parking lot consisted of sandy native soil, with a well-designed stone storage layer and reasonably effective infiltration capacity. Likewise, a pavement built on clay or a compacted subgrade may behave very differently.So the whole North Carolina research gives a more meaningful lesson than the headline alone. Permeable interlocking concrete pavers have the potential to greatly minimise runoff if the surface, stone layers, soil and maintenance techniques are suitable for the site. At Swansboro, such a combination allowed the pavement system to absorb an 88 mm rainfall event without producing measured surface runoff. The research showed that permeable concrete blocks can form part of an effective stormwater system when the pavement, storage layer, underlying soil and maintenance regime are suited to the site.You use AI every day. articles.summary: Three friends of Nolan Wells filed a defamation lawsuit against Terrell Owens over his X post demanding their arrest after the student's death.
articles.body: Three friends of Nolan Wells, the college student who disappeared from a Fourth of July celebration on a Mississippi island and was later found dead, have sued former NFL star Terrell Owens for defamation. The friends — Warren Hudson, Jax Pitalo and Morgan Seymour — accused the Hall of Fame wide receiver of defaming them after he posted on X: "ARREST THEM IMMEDIATELY!!" The fathers of the three friends filed the federal lawsuit on their sons' behalf Monday. All three are under 21, making them minors under Mississippi law. Hudson, Pitalo and Seymour were among a large group of friends who traveled by boat with 18-year-old Wells to Horn Island on the Fourth of July. The three all said Wells did not return to mainland Mississippi with the group because he was talking to a girl, an account his family has disputed. Wells' body was found two days later off the island's coast. NOLAN WELLS' FRIENDS CLEARED BY GRAND JURY AS THEIR LAWYERS VOW TO HOLD ONLINE ACCUSERS ACCOUNTABLE Images showing Wells, who was Black, with his white friends before his disappearance circulated widely online, with some social media users viewing the circumstances surrounding his death through a racial lens and directing suspicion toward his friends. Owens joined the public criticism in a Sept. 26 post that remains online. The post links to an Instagram reel by content creator Trent Out Loud that accused the three young men of deleting Snapchat messages from Wells' phone after his death while also suggesting they may have been responsible for killing him. However, Andrew Garrett, a digital forensics expert hired by attorney Benjamin Crump, examined Wells' phone and concluded that no one accessed it between 2:18 p.m. on July 4, when Wells last unlocked it, and 3:14 a.m. on July 5, when his parents gained access to the device. Garrett also clarified that Snapchat messages can disappear from a recipient's phone when they are remotely deleted by the person who sent them. 'THE WIND AND DRIFT PATTERNS TELL A STORY,' CAJUN NAVY OFFICIAL SAYS OF MISSING MISSISSIPPI TEEN FOUND DEAD In the lawsuit, the friends say Owens, 52, circulated a false narrative about them and accused them of crimes they did not commit. "The Defamatory X Post also placed Warren, Jax, and Morgan before Owens’ audience in a false light, as murderers and participants in a murder coverup who had escaped justice," according to the lawsuit. "There was absolutely no evidence to prompt an arrest of the Plaintiffs because they had done nothing wrong, and there was no probable cause to arrest Plaintiffs because they had not committed a crime." Fox News Digital reached out to Owens for comment through his social media accounts and SMAC Entertainment, which lists him as a client on its website. The grand jury did note that the state's autopsy report, which has not been made public, and an independent autopsy commissioned by the family found that Wells had bruising on the back of his head. The family's forensic pathologist, Roger A. Mitchell Jr., classified Wells' death as "undetermined," saying he could not rule out non-accidental factors because Wells did not appear too intoxicated to swim and had "apparent acute blunt force injuries to the head and body prior to his death." articles.title: Canada suspends plans to expand assisted dying to people with mental illness
articles.summary: People with mental illness alone were to be eligible for assisted dying in Canada in March 2027, but that has now been paused indefinitely.
articles.body:
Canada says it will indefinitely suspend plans to expand its medically assisted dying law to people whose sole condition is mental illness, citing a lack of consensus on who would be eligible.

It comes after a parliamentary panel earlier this year recommended that medically assisted dying - known as Maid in Canada - should not be expanded.

On Wednesday, Canada's justice minister, Sean Fraser, said that "while there is not a perfect consensus on this issue, we believe this is the correct approach at this particular time".

Supporters of extending the programme to those with mental illness alone argue that not doing so violates their constitutional rights and access to healthcare.

A federal case remains before the courts challenging the government's earlier decision to delay access to Maid for people with mental illness.

Fraser acknowledged this is an issue that the Supreme Court could weigh on in the future.

Wednesday's announcement means that Canadians with mental illness as their sole condition will not be able to access assisted dying by March 2027 as previously planned.

The government will instead introduce a new law in the coming weeks that suspends that expansion indefinitely, Fraser said.

That proposed legislation will also to allow patients who have a progressing incurable illness to consent to assisted dying before their health deteriorates to the point where they are unable to do so.

However, it will leave the final decision up to individual provinces.

Advanced requests are not currently legal under federal law, but are allowed in Quebec for those with serious and incurable illnesses.

"These are not easy decisions but we believe they will be the correct ones," Fraser said.

Medically assisted dying became legal in Canada in 2016 for people with terminal illnesses, who still account for the vast majority of cases.

Following a court case in Quebec, it was expanded in 2021 to people with incurable conditions but whose death was not imminent. In Canada, that mechanism is known as "track two" Maid.

Canada was first set to expand its assisted dying laws to people whose sole condition is mental illness in 2023, but it delayed doing so twice to allow for time to study its potential delivery.

Advocates for expanding assisted dying to people with mental illness alone say they should have the same rights as patients with other types of illness.

But concerns have been raised about whether mental illnesses are currently understood well enough by medicine to determine appropriate eligibility.

"When I hear that there is a lack of consensus in the medical community about the irremediable nature of certain mental illnesses, that gives me real cause for concern," Fraser said.

Canada should 'indefinitely exclude' people with mental illness from assisted dying, report says

What is a 'safe death'? Mentally ill woman asks for assisted dying in Canada

'I could live 30 years but plan to die': How assisted dying law is dividing Canadians

Claire Brosseau, a woman with treatment resistant bipolar 1 disorder who is part of the federal case challenging Canada's current laws, told the BBC earlier this year that assisted dying would offer her "a safe death".

Brosseau's lawyer, Michael Fenrick, told the BBC on Wednesday that the government's decision is "deeply disappointing".

"People will continue to suffer intolerably while the case goes through the courts," he said.

More broadly, some experts have also raised concerns that Canada's assisted dying programme has become a tool to alleviate the suffering of people who would be better served by improved access to affordable housing and healthcare, and not an option of last resort.

In a report earlier this year, a parliamentary committee noted competing opinions on the issue but recommended Canada "indefinitely exclude persons whose sole underlying medical condition is a mental illness" from assisted dying.

It added that there is a "pressing need for increased and more equitable access to adequate mental health services".

The conclusions were made after committee members heard from doctors, advocates and experts from countries that do allow assisted dying for people solely with mental illness, like the Netherlands and Belgium.

Not all committee members agreed with its recommendation, and some released a dissenting report arguing the process was "fundamentally flawed" and "biased".

Polls suggest the majority of Canadians support access to medically assisted death but that support falls it comes to patients with mental illness alone.

If you have been affected by any of the issues raised in this story, information and support can be found at the BBC's Action Line.

In Canada, support can be found at the Suicide Crisis Helpline by dialling 988

articles.title: Inheritance tax: What's in the Conservatives' plan and who benefits?
articles.summary: BBC Verify looks into the party's move to overhaul the tax that is levied on inherited wealth.
articles.body:
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has announced she will overhaul inheritance tax if her party wins the next general election.

She told the Conservatives' annual conference that "nobody will ever pay inheritance tax on their family home" and couples will be able to leave an additional £1m tax free.

Tax experts say the party's £6bn per year estimate of the cost of the plan is reasonable, but warn the policy would primarily benefit wealthier households and could discourage older people from moving to smaller homes.

BBC Verify has looked into the details of the policy.

Under the current system, inheritance tax of 40% is paid when someone's estate - the total value of their money and property exceeds £325,000. Anything under this amount is not taxed.

And, when a person dies, they can currently transfer this tax-free allowance to a surviving spouse or civil partner which increases the combined threshold for a couple to £650k.

On top of this individuals can get an additional transferable allowance for a family home of £175k each when it is left to children or other direct descendants.

So at present most married couples can potentially leave £1m without paying inheritance tax.

The Conservative plan would increase the £325,000 threshold - the point at which you start paying the tax - to £500,000 and fully exempt a family home from inheritance tax.

At the moment an estate with a £2m house could be liable for £400,000 in inheritance tax. That would reduce to zero under the Conservatives.

How many people currently pay inheritance tax?

Official figures show that in 2024-25 around 30,400 deaths in the UK left estates which were liable for inheritance tax.

This was around 5% of all UK deaths in that year.

But the number of estates paying inheritance tax is set to rise, due to the increasing value of inherited wealth being passed on and the threshold having been frozen.

The Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) has estimated that by 2032-33 around 12% of people will have inheritance tax due either on their own death or that of their spouse or civil partner.

Citing analysis by the consultancy Oxford Economics, the Conservatives say the number of estates paying the tax will rise to 52,100 in 2029-30.

How many people would benefit from the Conservative policy?

The Conservatives estimate their reforms would reduce the number of affected estates in 2030 to 22,000.

Official data shows higher value estates pay the majority of the inheritance tax collected.

The IFS has estimated that if inheritance tax were to be entirely scrapped, which Badenoch has identified as a longer term aspiration, the wealthiest 1% of estates - those worth £2.1m or more - would get half of the benefit of the tax reduction.

And one long-standing criticism of inheritance tax is that the wealthy use legal ways to avoid paying it like putting their assets into family trusts to reduce the amount of inheritance tax ultimately due from their estates when they die.

In 2023-24, estates with a valuation of £10m only paid an average effective inheritance tax rate of 18%, according to estimates from HM Revenue and Customs.

Responding to Wednesday's conference announcement, the IFS said: "The biggest beneficiaries would be those with the highest wealth and the most valuable homes – and their descendants.

"This is a very well-off group, mainly living in London and the South-East of England."

The Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR), the official forecaster, estimates inheritance tax will raise £9.5bn in 2026-27 - equivalent to around 0.3% of GDP.

The OBR projects this will rise to £14.5bn in 2030-31 or 0.4% of GDP.

The Conservatives estimate their plan would cost £6bn a year in 2029-30, based on Oxford Economics' analysis.

The party says it has identified £71bn in annual savings including £36bn a year from welfare cuts.

Prof Andy Summers, director of the Centre for the Analysis of Taxation, told BBC Verify this was "just about about the worst possible way to deliver an inheritance tax cut".

"Exempting the family home however much it's worth will just encourage older people to concentrate their savings in their home, prevent downsizing, and so further gum up the housing market," he said.

The Conservatives argue in their press release accompanying the policy announcement that inheritance taxes are "bad for growth".

But analysis by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development suggests inheritance taxes in general are less damaging to economic growth than taxes on income from work.

articles.title: Conservatives united behind Kemi Badenoch - but party still needs to win over voters
articles.summary: Kemi Badenoch has the support of her party but the Tories still trail Labour and Reform in opinion polls.
articles.body:
It is Kemi Badenoch's Conservative Party now.

Implicitly and explicitly, that was the message from the Tories' annual conference, which has wrapped up in Birmingham.

It is a party very much united around her, with no murmurings of dissent about her leadership, which is quite the contrast from a year ago.

The pivot point in her time as Conservative leader so far came in her address to this same gathering 12 months back, when, amid constant chatter about the prospect of Robert Jenrick seeking to topple her, she won over the party faithful with an address that oozed confidence.

Not just that. Us reporters were given her speech script, allowing us to follow it line-by-line to help us report what she has said quickly and accurately. But there was a page missing towards the end. On that page was the Conservative crowd pleaser of a plan to scrap stamp duty in England and Northern Ireland .

Fast forward to now and there was a familiar drill. There was plenty of chat throughout the conference and beforehand of a new policy coming on inheritance tax, and, sure enough, another page was missing towards the end of her speech with her plan on that.

The plan reopens the fascinating politics and psychology of inheritance tax – which is paid by fewer than one in 20 people but has been described as the country's most unpopular tax .

Why so? Advocates of cutting or scrapping it say it is because plenty aspire to one day being rich enough to end up having to pay it, plus it is a second tax on already taxed income.

But the Conservatives' opponents, even before this speech, were already looking forward to the argument they anticipated after it.

Reform UK, for instance, claim it is a "tax cut for multi-millionaires" and that their plan to cut income tax for millions by raising the threshold at which most people start paying it will benefit far more people.

Badenoch pledges inheritance tax changes as she pitches Tories as 'no-nonsense' party

What's in the Conservatives' inheritance tax plan and who benefits?

I'd rather have another election than do a deal with Reform UK, says Badenoch

Policy announcements aside, what stood out in this speech for me was a broader point. The veteran Conservative elections strategist Sir Lynton Crosby once suggested the party ought to "scrape the barnacles off the boat" as he put it, in reference to unpopular policies that could cause the Tories a headache during an election campaign.

This speech felt like Badenoch revelling in pointing at the clean hull of the Conservative ship, what she sees as those barnacles removed, not least the high-profile defections of Jenrick and Suella Braverman.

There was a striking glee and anger in her reflections about Reform UK. She sought to portray them as sleazy and pointedly decided to lean into an argument of recent months about Englishness.

Braverman has argued that, given her Asian heritage, "I'm not English".

"I'm proud to be British. My family and ancestors have a link to Britain which spans centuries. But in no way are we English," she wrote on social media last month , adding: "Englishness is an ethnicity."

Badenoch expressed her personal fury at this, saying that as the mother of mixed-race children "I don't want to explain to my son, when we're watching our brilliant England team play football, that some people don't think our black players are English".

The recurring message, today and over the last few days, is Badenoch cannot stand Reform and won't work with them before or after the next general election.

But what she said amounted to an attack on Reform's character and the judgement of their prominent figures, rather than a significant focus on the policies we hear talked about most often by Nigel Farage.

Badenoch did talk about immigration, but not at length. She largely left the issue – and the Conservative policy to withdraw from the European Convention on Human Rights, as Reform also advocates - to her shadow home secretary Chris Philp who spoke before her.

Instead, Badenoch grounded this speech in the big picture tussle to be trusted between Labour and the Conservatives – and in particular who was better placed to deliver a growing economy.

In tone, language and public enthusiasm for the argument, Badenoch and Andy Burnham are quite the contrast with their immediate predecessors Rishi Sunak and Sir Keir Starmer.

Badenoch and Burnham both look like they are enjoying themselves on the stage, and are both enthusiastic purveyors of the core of what are their very different worldviews.

Badenoch acknowledged this with what she called the "battle for the soul of this nation" in the opening minute or so of her address. It is a trailer for the debate to come this autumn and beyond.

The Conservatives feel chipper and are united. But while both of these things are better than the alternative for any party leader, they are not the same as being popular.

And, as Kemi Badenoch acknowledged, they are not there on that score yet, by a long chalk, with opinion polls suggesting they are more unpopular than when they were annihilated at the last general election.

The numbers, for them, are dire. Just not as bad, relatively speaking, as they were.

But they hope things are looking up for them: Reform has had a bruising few months, and Labour, they believe, are leaning to the Left, trying to lure Green and Liberal Democrat supporters towards them.

Can the Conservatives also lure recent Lib Dem supporters in the south of England with talk of help with childcare costs whatever your income , not hiking the council tax of very expensive homes and this inheritance tax plan?

This, Tories hope, there are now gaps in the political market they can exploit.

They crave catching and overtaking Reform in the polls, in the hope that after that there is a tipping point allowing them to credibly claim they are the most viable alternative to a Labour or Labour-led future government. Let's see.

B.A.S.S. flips a coin to determine LiveScope use in 2027 The timing of Gallant's comments is especially interesting now that we know exactly when Elite Series anglers will — and won't — have access to the technology next season. B.A.S.S. revealed the results of its 2027 live-sonar coin flips Tuesday, and perhaps the most intriguing result is Lake St. Clair. When the Elite Series visits the famed smallmouth fishery Aug. 5-8, forward-facing sonar will be prohibited. That's notable because St. Clair has become closely associated with the electronics-driven techniques that have transformed modern smallmouth fishing. It'll also be the eighth event of the season, with Angler of the Year points and Bassmaster Classic qualification increasingly important. The coin also determined that live sonar will be allowed at the 2027 Bassmaster Classic on Lake Hartwell, while the 2028 Classic will be contested without it. Gallant will have to compete under both sets of rules next season. And while he's certainly not giving up his electronics when they're allowed, he admitted there's something to be said for fishing without them. Cooper Gallant says fishing can be more fun without LiveScope Gallant gave me a crash course in LiveScope while we were fishing Table Rock Lake in Missouri last week. Watch the full video here: For those who don't know, forward-facing sonar allows anglers to see what's happening beneath the water in real time. Instead of simply casting toward a promising spot and hoping there's a fish hanging around, an angler can use the technology to locate fish and even watch how they react to a lure. "This transducer basically shoots wherever my trolling motor is facing," Gallant explained. "I have it set at 120 feet, so I can see 120 feet out in front of me." Fish, trees, rocks — whatever is down there, he can see it. And, more importantly, he can see what the fish does next. "You can see your bait, you can see the fish react to your bait," he said. "It's all in real time." That's obviously incredibly useful when you're trying to make a living catching bass. It's also a heck of a time-saver. Of course, not every tournament allows LiveScope. So I asked Gallant whether fishing without all that technology feels like a welcome challenge or a daunting task. Turns out, he actually enjoys it. "I think sometimes without it, it’s more fun," Gallant said. "There’s more unknown. You don’t know if there’s a fish there, and when you get a bite, it’s more of a surprise." That's a pretty interesting admission from someone who competes at the highest level of a sport that has spent the past several years arguing about this exact technology. Without LiveScope, you might know you're fishing a good-looking spot. You might have a pretty good idea there are bass nearby. But you don't get to watch the whole thing unfold on a screen before the bite ever happens. Gallant isn't saying he'd throw his electronics overboard. Far from it. "It's incredible technology," he said. He's simply acknowledging something plenty of recreational anglers probably understand. The most efficient way to catch a fish isn't necessarily the most fun way to catch one. Sometimes there's something to be said for chucking a lure into the water and having absolutely no idea what's about to happen. LiveScope isn't going anywhere in professional bass fishing Of course, Gallant doesn't have the luxury of approaching every day on the water like a casual Sunday fishing trip with a novice like me. For professional anglers, technology is part of the job. And when I asked him about some veteran anglers' reluctance to embrace forward-facing sonar, he was sympathetic — to a point. "I think the older generation, they're just hesitant to learn it," Gallant said. "But it's just like anything. The sport evolves." And so does the technology. Gallant said younger anglers may have an advantage simply because many of them grew up learning to fish with advanced electronics. But for anyone trying to compete at the highest level, ignoring that evolution isn't much of an option. "You have to learn it, or you're going to get left behind," he said. That's not a new position for Gallant, either. Before the 2025 Elite Series season, he wrote for Bassmaster that professional anglers had to adopt forward-facing sonar when LiveScope arrived to avoid falling behind their competition. Still, B.A.S.S. has spent the past year experimenting with what competition looks like when anglers don't have access to it. COOPER GALLANT SLEPT IN HIS TRUCK FOR YEARS CHASING PRO FISHING DREAM: 'I DIDN'T HAVE A PLAN B' In 2026, the organization introduced a split format for the Elite Series, with forward-facing sonar permitted at five of nine regular-season tournaments and prohibited at the other four. Lake Guntersville, where FFS was prohibited, became the most-watched Elite event of the regular season with more than 21 million minutes viewed across B.A.S.S. digital platforms. The St. Lawrence River finale, where anglers could use FFS, was second with more than 20 million minutes viewed. B.A.S.S. apparently liked the balance. The organization announced last month that the 50/50 format will return for 2027, with Tuesday's coin flip determining which events land on which side. For the first time, the Bassmaster Classic is getting the same treatment: One flip will determine whether forward-facing sonar is allowed at the 2027 Classic, with the opposite rules automatically applying in 2028. Now we know how that split will look in 2027. Live sonar will be permitted at Lake Okeechobee, Lake Fork, Santee Cooper Lakes, the Tennessee-Tombigbee Waterway and the Mississippi River. It will be prohibited at Kissimmee Chain of Lakes, the Sabine River, Lake Seminole and Lake St. Clair. And for the first time, the Classic will join the experiment. Live sonar will be allowed at the 2027 Bassmaster Classic on Lake Hartwell, while the technology will be banned at the 2028 Classic, regardless of where that tournament is ultimately held. It's an interesting compromise for a sport still figuring out exactly how much technology it wants at its highest level. And Gallant's perspective might be a pretty good summary of the whole debate. SIGN UP FOR THE DAILY OUTKICK NEWSLETTER LiveScope can make you more efficient. It can show you fish you might never have known were there. At the professional level, learning how to use it can be the difference between keeping up and getting left behind. But take it away? And hey, you might just have a little more fun. articles.title: From 2 categories to 4: Waste segregation changes in Hubballi-Dharwad
articles.summary: Hubballi-Dharwad households must now segregate waste into wet, dry, sanitary and hazardous categories; HDMC to retrofit 336 auto tippers with extra bins.
articles.body: ​Hubballi: Households in Hubballi-Dharwad will segregate waste into four categories under the Solid Waste Management Rules-2026, with sanitary and special concern/hazardous waste to be collected separately in addition to wet and dry waste.The Hubballi-Dharwad Municipal Corporation (HDMC) plans to modify its collection system accordingly. The 336 auto tippers operating in the twin cities, which currently have arrangements for wet and dry waste, will be fitted with two additional bins. A tender will be floated after the Model Code of Conduct (MCC) is lifted, and the vehicles are expected to be retrofitted within two months.The four categories were displayed during the Swachhata Hi Seva programme.Under the 2026 rules, sanitary waste includes diapers and clothes, while special concern/hazardous waste includes glass, bulbs, batteries, medicine bottles, paint cans, disinfectant cans, used needles and syringes. Used medical syringes, insulin needles and chemical containers are frequently being mixed with dry waste, posing health and safety risks.Santosh Yarangalli, executive engineer of HDMC’s solid waste management department, told TOI that compliance with the Solid Waste Management Rules-2026 Act is mandatory and came into effect on April 1, 2026. Every household must now segregate and dispose of four types of waste. Public directives require collecting and disposing of wet waste, dry waste, sanitary waste, and hazardous waste separately.”Until now, according to the Solid Waste Management Rules-2016, it was mandatory to segregate only wet (kitchen and vegetable) and dry waste (recyclable plastic, paper, metal, etc.). However, four types of waste now need to be collected separately, requiring updates to our infrastructure,” Yarangalli explained.He noted that existing auto tippers currently only have arrangements for wet and dry waste. Under the new rules, each vehicle needs two additional bins. The 336 auto tippers operating in the twin cities will be modified accordingly. A tender will be called soon, and the vehicles are expected to be retrofitted within two months.The twin cities of Hubballi-Dharwad generate approximately 400 to 600 tonnes of solid waste every day combined.GFXWhat goes where?Green - Wet: Kitchen, vegetable wasteBlue - Dry: Plastic, paper, metalYellow - Sanitary: Diapers, clothesRed - Hazardous: Glass, bulbs, batteries, medicine bottles, paint/disinfectant cans, used needles, syringesStay updated with the latest Hubballi news. articles.title: Illegal coracle rides flourish despite safety warnings at Hampi
articles.summary: Illegal coracle rides continue near Sanapur across from Hampi despite bans and safety warnings, with officials planning raids, FIRs and seizure of boats.
articles.body: Koppal: Unauthorised coracle rides continue on the Tungabhadra river near Sanapur in Gangavathi, across from Hampi, despite restrictions and repeated notices to operators, raising concerns over tourist safety in Hampi.Villagers alleged that operators had openly resumed rides near the old tourist bungalow, Sanapur parallel reservoir and waterfalls after the district administration and irrigation department restricted them. Sanapur, known as Mini Goa, attracts tourists from India and abroad. Resorts in Sanapur, Hanumanahalli, Anegundi, Kishkindha and Jangli allegedly direct visitors to the riverbank and encourage coracle rides.Operators charge local tourists Rs 800 to Rs 1,000 per ride, regular visitor Veeresh Ballari said. Coracles have capsized in the area in the past, while repeated police warnings have failed to stop the activity, he added. A Gangavathi Rural police officer, speaking on condition of anonymity, said complaints alleged that operators charged Rs 5,000 to Rs 8,000 for pre-wedding shoots, with a minimum fee of Rs 5,000.Villagers questioned the selective enforcement of restrictions. Forest department warning boards advise people against entering the river because of crocodiles and otters, while Sanapur gram panchayat has prohibited washing clothes there. Some visitors allegedly cross the river by coracle in the morning, consume alcohol and food on the opposite bank, and return in the evening, villagers said.Irrigation department assistant executive engineer Amaresh Kampli said repeated notices had failed to stop the rides. Gangavathi taluk panchayat executive officer Ramareddy Patil said the revenue, forest and irrigation departments and taluk panchayat would conduct a joint operation and file complaints against operators.Gangavathi range forest officer Basavaraj said a complaint had been lodged with Rural Police Station. An FIR would be registered and coracles seized as operators continued rides while evading officials, he said. Villagers urged the district administration and police, irrigation and forest departments to coordinate action to avert a possible tragedy.Stay updated with the latest Hubballi news. articles.title: Grocery shoppers may be relying on a 'misleading' clue when choosing healthy foods
articles.summary: Shoppers view foods with shorter shelf lives as more natural, but UBC Sauder research reveals packaging technology often explains the difference.
articles.body: A shorter shelf life may make food seem fresher and healthier, but new research suggests that may be more perception than reality. A study from the University of British Columbia (UBC) Sauder School of Business in Canada found that many shoppers use a food's shelf life as a shortcut for judging how natural it is, even though longer shelf lives can reflect factors beyond heavy processing. The team, which included researchers from China, conducted a series of experiments in which participants compared foods with different shelf lives, including potato chips, pasta sauce, mayonnaise and granola bars. YOUR BRAIN MAY BE TRICKING YOU INTO LIKING ARTIFICIAL SWEETENERS, STUDY FINDS Shoppers consistently viewed foods with shorter shelf lives as more natural and healthier, even when the ingredients and nutritional facts were nearly identical or the difference in shelf life was solely due to better packaging. In the case of the mayonnaise, the only difference between the two products was that one had a better seal, allowing it to stay fresh longer — it was no more processed than the other. Yet participants still viewed the shorter-shelf-life option as more natural. Even when they were given clear indications that a longer-lasting product just had better packaging, shoppers still used shelf life as a gauge, the researchers found. JUST ONE SMALL SERVING OF ULTRA-PROCESSED FOOD A DAY LINKED TO HIGHER DISEASE RISK, MAJOR STUDY FINDS In other experiments, participants rated potato chips with a five-month shelf life as more natural and healthier than nearly identical chips with a nine-month shelf life. Nearly 70% of participants selected a pasta sauce with a one-year shelf life when they were encouraged to prioritize natural foods. That figure dropped to 43% when the emphasis shifted to reducing food waste and protecting the environment, as the researchers found that participants also associated longer shelf life with less waste because items wouldn't go bad as quickly. The findings, published in the Journal of Consumer Psychology earlier this year, suggest shoppers often use shelf life as a "mental shortcut" when making purchasing decisions, researchers said. AMERICANS ARE DITCHING ULTRA-PROCESSED SNACKS FOR AN ANCIENT FRUIT THAT'S EXPLODING IN POPULARITY "Our research shows consumers are using shelf life as a shortcut for judging whether foods are natural," co-author Yann Cornil, an associate professor at UBC Sauder, told Fox News Digital. "It sometimes can be diagnostic, but shelf life is also very much dependent on the quality of the packaging, which has nothing to do with food naturalness." Cornil added that the shortcut can be "misleading." THIS AMOUNT OF DELI MEAT ASSOCIATED WITH HIGHER DEMENTIA RISK IN COMPELLING NEW REVIEW Packaging has improved dramatically, he noted, just like refrigeration did 60 years ago, to improve food preservation. "Don't judge a food by its shelf life." The tendency to equate a shorter shelf life with less processing may have unintended consequences, according to the researchers. Buyers may therefore skip products that are just as healthy while choosing items that are more likely to spoil before they can be eaten. Products like canned beans, frozen fruits and vegetables and dried oats can stay fresh for months or even years thanks to preservation methods and packaging rather than added ingredients. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE STORIES "A shorter shelf life does not automatically mean a food is healthier," Kelly Springer, a New York-based registered dietitian and founder and CEO of Kelly's Choice, told Fox News Digital. "Better seals, oxygen barriers and moisture-control packaging help foods stay fresh longer while maintaining quality and safety." Springer pointed to some packaged items such as guacamole, which can have a longer refrigerated shelf life because of high-pressure processing and packaging technology rather than added preservatives, yet are still healthy choices. Other items such as milk, yogurt and kefir can stay fresh longer due to pasteurization and fermentation — not necessarily added ingredients. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ "Don't judge a food by its shelf life," Springer, who was not involved in the research, added. "Turn the package over, read the nutrition label and make decisions based on what's inside." She recommends consumers focus on fiber, protein, added sugar and sodium rather than the expiration date alone. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER Cornil added that saturated fat content can also be problematic. "Too many ingredients, in particular ingredients [such as] additives and preservatives that you can't recognize, or can't even pronounce, may be a signal of too much processing and unhealthiness," Cornil said. "It's not always true, but I would say that it is more diagnostic than shelf life information." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The findings are especially relevant as many seek to reduce how much ultra-processed food they eat. Roughly 55% of Americans' daily caloric intake is from ultra-processed foods, the researchers noted.

articles.title: Nandini milk price hike worries residents, stakeholders in Mysuru
articles.summary: Mysuru residents and businesses worry as Karnataka govt plans an Rs 8/litre Nandini milk hike; farmers seek full benefit and pending Rs 5 incentive.
articles.body: Mysuru: State govt’s decision to raise Nandini milk prices by at least Rs 8 per litre has sparked concern among consumers and businesses, while milk producers have demanded that the entire benefit be transferred to them.Farmers also sought timely release of the Rs 5-per-litre incentive for milk supplied to Karnataka Milk Federation (KMF). They said milk production was a major livelihood amid crop losses after the district recorded a rainfall deficit of over 59% during the southwest monsoon.Karnataka Rajya Raitha Sangha Mysuru district unit president Hosur Kumar, who supplies about 20 litres of milk to KMF, said the incentive had not been released for five months.“The price hike is required. But our demand is that the entire amount must be transferred to the milk producers,” he said. “Currently, We get an average Rs 32 per litre of milk we supply to dairy,” he added.MYMUL managing director KN Suresh Naik said the union had 2,25,000 milk producers and collected an average of 10.5 lakh kilolitres of milk daily, with the highest collection reaching 11.5 lakh kilolitres. Farmers received Rs 32.2 per litre, he said.Hotel Owner’s Association president C Narayana Gowda said Nandini ghee prices had already risen twice in recent months. He feared the milk price increase would raise prices of curd, buttermilk, paneer and other byproducts, severely affecting hotels.“We are not against price hike. But it should be moderate.
